story: The Colorado Springs Pioneers Museum sits in a granite building with a domed clock tower. It was the El Paso County Courthouse from 1903 to 1973, and the museum moved in during 1979. The building is on the National Register of Historic Places, and was the second property in El Paso County to be listed, after Pikes Peak.

More than 60,000 objects fill the collection, from Arapaho, Cheyenne and Ute artifacts to Van Briggle pottery, quilts and items that belonged to writer Helen Hunt Jackson. The museum also holds papers of General William Jackson Palmer, the city's founder. Admission is free.
The museum sits within Alamo Square Park. A street clock from 1900 stands there too, saved from being destroyed during urban renewal in the 1960s.
stops.fact: The building was the county courthouse for 70 years.
stops.disputed: Many people assume a courthouse was always a courthouse. Wikipedia says this one has been a museum since 1979.

claims.t: The building was the El Paso County Courthouse from 1903 to 1973.
Admission to the museum costs a lot of money.

story: Seven Falls is a series of seven waterfalls on South Cheyenne Creek, in a 1,000-foot (300 m) granite canyon in Colorado Springs. It has been a privately owned tourist attraction since it opened in the early 1880s. The canyon entrance is about 4.5 miles southwest of downtown.

The heights of the seven falls add up to 181 feet (55 m), and a staircase of 224 steps climbs from the base to the top. An elevator goes up to the Eagle's Nest viewing platform. Wikipedia says Seven Falls is Colorado's only waterfall on the National Geographic list of international waterfalls.
Two trails start at the top of the falls. One leads to Inspiration Point, a favorite spot of the writer Helen Hunt Jackson, who was originally buried there.
stops.fact: The seven falls are named in alphabetical order.
stops.disputed: Many people assume the falls are named from top to bottom. Wikipedia says they are named in alphabetical order, not top to bottom.

story: Garden of the Gods is a 1,341.3-acre (542.8 ha) public park in Colorado Springs. About 862 acres of it were designated a National Natural Landmark in 1971. Its red rock formations were created millions of years ago during the Laramide Orogeny.

The Europeans first called the area Red Rock Corral. Wikipedia says that in August 1859 two surveyors, Melancthon Beach and Rufus Cable, explored the site. Beach thought it was a capital place for a beer garden. Cable said it was a fit place for the gods to assemble, and the name stuck.

Archaeological evidence shows that prehistoric people visited about 1330 BC, and many native peoples report a connection to the place, including the Apache, Cheyenne, Comanche, Kiowa, Lakota, Pawnee, Shoshone and Ute.
stops.fact: The park has been used by people for over 3,000 years.
stops.disputed: Many people repeat one story of how the park got its name. Wikipedia says an 1893 newspaper credited Helen Hunt Jackson instead, so the story is disputed.

claims.t: The name 'Garden of the Gods' was suggested in 1859 by surveyor Rufus Cable.
claims.why: Wikipedia gives that account of the naming.

claims.t: The red rocks were created in the last century.
claims.why: Wikipedia says they formed millions of years ago.

story: Pikes Peak, also called America's Mountain, is a fourteener with a summit of 14,115 feet (4,302 m). It is the easternmost fourteener in the United States. The base is in Manitou Springs, 10 miles west of downtown Colorado Springs.

Zebulon Pike was ordered by Thomas Jefferson in 1806 to explore the Louisiana Purchase. He tried to climb the mountain that winter but gave up, possibly because of the cold. The first documented hike to the top was by Edwin James on July 15, 1820. The mountain was later named for Pike by newspapers during the gold rush.

In 1893, visiting professor and poet Katharine Lee Bates climbed to the summit and was inspired to write 'America the Beautiful'. Its first title was 'Pikes Peak'. The Ute people called the mountain Tava, meaning sun.
stops.fact: The mountain is the easternmost fourteener in the United States.
stops.disputed: Many people think Zebulon Pike reached the top. Wikipedia says he abandoned his climb, and the first documented hike was Edwin James in 1820.

claims.t: The first documented hike to the summit was in 1820.
Zebulon Pike reached the summit in 1806.
claims.why: Wikipedia says he abandoned the climb.
